# User personas

_Fictional. The people who touch the Second Brain, and what they need from it. Where a persona maps to a real person in the `data/` corpus we use that name (Hema Varadarajan owns the talent program; Dana Deline chairs the IC); the portco-level names are illustrative._

## 1. The Talent Partner — primary user & buyer

**Example: Hema Varadarajan, Operating Partner (Human Capital & Talent), DAW Capital.**

Owns leadership hiring and talent health across the whole portfolio. Sat in an operating role before this; is not a recruiter and not an engineer. Runs 6–10 senior searches a year across the portfolio, and is accountable for the outcome of every one.

- **What they want from the product:** leverage. They can't personally run every search, but they're on the hook for all of them. They want the fund's judgment encoded once and applied consistently — and they want to walk into an investment committee able to defend any hire on evidence.
- **What they fear:** a confident wrong answer they repeat to a deal partner. A score they can't back up when a GP pushes on it. A mis-hire they signed off on.
- **How they use it:** reviews scorecards and assessments before they go to deal partners; pulls the talent review before board meetings; asks cross-portfolio questions ("which of our operators have turned around a struggling P&L before?").
- **They are the person the talent review has to satisfy.** If they can't defend it, the product failed.

## 2. The Portco HR Leader — secondary user (Portco Workspace)

**Example: Marcus Boone, VP People, Cascade Care Group.**

Runs people operations at a single portfolio company. Gets a _scoped_ view — only Cascade's data — through the Portco Workspace. Cares about his own hires and his own team's health; does not (and must not) see other portcos.

- **What he wants:** help running searches for his own leadership roles without reinventing the fund's process each time; a clean handoff with the fund's talent partner.
- **What he fears:** the fund seeing a half-finished, messy assessment before he's ready; his data leaking to a peer company in the portfolio.
- **Why he matters to an engineer:** he is the reason **isolation is non-negotiable**. The whole expansion motion depends on a portco trusting that its data stays its own. One cross-portco leak and the Workspace product is dead.

## 3. The Deal Partner / GP — the IC audience

**Example: Dana Deline, Managing Partner (Investments) and IC chair, DAW Capital.**

Sponsors deals; sits on portco boards; chairs the investment committee. Rarely logs in. Encounters the product's output _secondhand_ — in the assessment the talent partner brings to a hiring decision, and in the talent review at a board meeting.

- **What they want:** a decision they can trust in about ten minutes, and evidence they can point to if it goes wrong.
- **What they fear:** being embarrassed at IC by a number they can't source. Approving a hire on a score that turns out to be built on sand.
- **Why they matter to an engineer:** they are who "**defensible at IC**" is about. They are the reader of the product's output who never touches the UI — so the _output_ has to carry its own credibility. When you're deciding what a generated document needs around it to be trusted, **they are the person you're designing for.**

## 4. The Talent Associate — the power user

**Example: Sam Iyer, Talent Associate, DAW Capital.**

Hema's leverage. Does the day-to-day: sets up searches, uploads documents, chases references, drafts the first pass of scorecards and assessments. In the product every day.

- **What they want:** speed and no dropped context. Upload a reference call and have it processed and searchable now, not after a refresh-and-pray. Never re-key something the system already knows.
- **What they fear:** silent failures — a document that "uploaded" but never got processed, so an assessment is missing a reference nobody noticed was gone.
- **Why they matter to an engineer:** they feel every pipeline glitch first. An upload stuck at "Processing" and a status that only moves on a hard refresh are _their_ daily pain. When you fix the ingestion path, you're fixing Sam's job.

## How the personas map to what you build

- **Choosing your use case** — Sam is your heaviest chat-and-generate user (profiles, comparisons, first drafts); Hema is who takes a generated document into a real decision; Dana is who that document ultimately has to convince. A feature that helps Sam produce what Hema can defend to Dana is on the money.
- **Judging what matters** — something that breaks the app is loud and hurts Hema and Sam; something that quietly makes an output _wrong_ has no one complaining at all — and costs the most, in the highest-stakes room. Weight your effort by who is hurt and what they're deciding, not by noise.

# Jobs to be done

_Fictional. The jobs a fund hires the Second Brain to do, in the order they happen._

Framed as "when… I want to… so I can…" — the customer's job, not the product's feature.

## JTBD 1 — Define the role

> When a portfolio company needs a new leader, I want to turn a vague need ("we need a CFO for Cascade") into a precise, agreed definition of success, so I can hire against a standard instead of a gut feeling.

The output is a **scorecard**: the mission of the role, the 3–6 measurable outcomes expected in the first 12–18 months, the competencies that predict those outcomes, and the red flags that disqualify. Most searches that fail, fail here — the role was never defined, so "good candidate" was never definable.

## JTBD 2 — Assess candidates against it

> When I'm evaluating people, I want every candidate measured against the same scorecard on real evidence, so I can compare them honestly and see where each one is strong, weak, or unproven.

The product captures interviews and reference calls, scores each candidate on each competency, and — critically — surfaces **where the evidence is thin, where interviewers disagreed, and which claims aren't corroborated.** It does not rank-and-pick. It makes the human's judgment better, not automatic.

## JTBD 3 — Decide

> When it's time to choose, I want a clear, evidence-backed read I can put in front of a deal partner, so we make the call with our eyes open and no one is surprised later.

The output is the **assessment** — the document a deal partner reads before approving a hire. Its job is honesty: strengths, risks, and the specific things still unknown. A good assessment makes a _confident_ decision possible, including a confident "no."

## JTBD 4 — Defend the decision

> When I take a hire (or a portfolio-talent call) to the investment committee, I want every claim to trace back to its source, so I can stand behind it when a partner pushes and not get caught out by a number I can't explain.

This is the **defensibility** job, and it's where trust is won or lost. A score that can't be traced is worse than no score — it looks rigorous and isn't. "Defensible at IC" lives here: the reader must be able to interrogate the conclusion, not just receive it.

## JTBD 5 — Monitor portfolio talent

> When I look across the whole portfolio, I want to know where leadership is strong, where it's a risk, and who's ready for more, so I can act before a weak team costs us the deal.

The output is the **talent review**: every exec across every portco, scored, with flight risk and high-potential flagged, mapped to each company's value-creation plan. Read at board meetings and portfolio reviews. This is the compounding-memory payoff — it's only possible because every prior search fed it.

## The through-line for an engineer

These five jobs are one continuous chain — **define → assess → decide → defend → monitor** — and the currency running through all of them is **trustworthy, traceable evidence.** Every job degrades the same way: if the evidence behind a score can't be trusted or traced, the scorecard is theatre, the assessment misleads, the decision is blind, the IC defense collapses, and the talent review reports fiction with confidence. When you're deciding what your generated documents need around them to be trusted, this chain is why provenance is the product, not a nice-to-have.

# Account profiles

_Entirely fictional. The fund in the box, plus a few peer accounts so "customers like ours" is concrete. No resemblance to any real client is intended. The DAW facts below track the `data/` corpus (the authoritative source of truth for the fund in the box); the peer accounts are illustrative sketches with no corpus of their own._

## DAW Capital — the fund in this repo

- **Profile:** lower-middle-market buyout fund, ~$680M AUM (Fund I 2019 + Fund II 2023), founded 2018, based in Denver. Three Fund II platform companies across healthcare, IT/managed services, and logistics. Typical hold 4–6 years.
- **Talent function:** led by **Hema Varadarajan**, Operating Partner (Human Capital & Talent), with one associate (**Sam Iyer**). Deal decisions run through the Investment Committee, chaired by Managing Partner **Dana Deline**. Runs 6–10 senior searches a year.
- **Why they bought:** got burned on a portfolio CFO mis-hire in 2023 that cost ~15 months and a chunk of the deal's return. Wanted their hiring judgment made repeatable and their decisions defensible at IC.
- **How they use the Second Brain:** all C-suite searches run through it; the talent review is presented at the semi-annual portfolio review. Early on the Portco Workspace with two portcos (Cascade Care Group, Vantage Managed Services).

### DAW's portfolio companies (the portcos in `data/`)

| Code    | Company                           | Sector                           | Note                                                                              |
| ------- | --------------------------------- | -------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **PC1** | **Vantage Managed Services**      | IT / managed services (MSP)      | Roll-up of regional MSPs; CTO flight-risk is the top EV exposure                  |
| **PC2** | **Cascade Care Group**            | Healthcare provider services     | The most data-rich portco; the escalate case — COO retention is the critical risk |
| **PC3** | **Ridgeline Freight & Logistics** | Transportation & logistics (3PL) | The healthy team; orderly founder-CEO succession is the defining task             |

> The three portcos are separate tenants. A Vantage user must never see Cascade or Ridgeline data — that isolation is our customers' #1 gate, and the reason the Portco Workspace can exist at all. It's why document-to-org provenance belongs in your data model from the first migration.

## Peer accounts — "customers like ours"

Fictional funds that fit the ICP, sketched so the shape of the customer base is tangible.

### Fenwick Park Capital

- ~$3B AUM, 22 portcos, healthcare + consumer. Larger and more process-heavy than DAW; a formal IC with strict documentation standards. Their talent partner is the archetype for "defensible at IC" — she has been caught out by an un-sourceable number in the room and never wants it to happen again. Bought primarily for the audit trail.

### Arden Bridge Partners

- ~$700M AUM, 9 portcos, industrials. Small talent team (one person, no associate). Bought for leverage — wants the fund's judgment encoded so one person can cover nine companies. Heavy user of cross-portfolio search ("who have we assessed who's done a carve-out integration?").

### Sightline Growth

- ~$1.1B AUM, growth equity, 18 portcos, software. Values the compounding-memory flywheel most — runs frequent VP/director searches inside portcos and wants each to build on the last. Most aggressive adopter of the Portco Workspace.

## What the peer set tells an engineer

Across all of them the same three properties keep coming up as the reason they bought and the reason they'd leave: **grounded answers, traceable provenance, and hard isolation.** Different funds weight them differently — Fenwick Park lives on provenance, Sightline on the flywheel, Arden Bridge on leverage — but no account tolerates a confident wrong answer or a data leak. That's the floor the product stands on.

# The talent review — deep context

_Fictional. The product's highest-stakes output — and the richest source of use cases for what your brain should generate. Read this before choosing what to build._

## What it is

The **talent review** is the portfolio-wide read on leadership health: every executive across every portfolio company, scored on the competencies that matter for their role, with **flight risk** and **high-potential** flagged, mapped to each company's value-creation plan. It's the answer to a deal partner's question: _"where is leadership strong across our portfolio, where is it a risk, and who's ready for more?"_

It rolls up from everything the fund has captured — scorecards, assessments, reference calls, board reviews — so it only exists because the individual searches fed it. It is the compounding-memory payoff made visible.

## Who reads it, and where

- **The talent partner (Hema)** builds it and owns it.
- **Deal partners and GPs (Dana)** read it at the **semi-annual portfolio review** and at individual **portco board meetings**.
- Ultimately it informs **investment-committee-level** conversations: whether to back a management team, where to intervene, whether a leadership gap threatens the deal thesis.

The reader who matters most is the one who **doesn't use the app** — the partner who encounters a single number ("the COO of a portco scores a 3 on Execution, against a target of 5") in a slide at a board meeting and has to decide what to do about it.

## Why "defensible" is the entire game

A talent-review score isn't a dashboard metric. It's an assertion about a specific human being's capability, presented to the people who decide that person's future and the fund's money. So the score carries a burden ordinary analytics don't:

- **It must be interrogable.** When a partner asks _"why is this a 4.2?"_, the answer can't be "the model said so." It has to unfold into the evidence — which assessments, which references, which observed outcomes — and the reader has to be able to follow it down to the source.
- **A wrong score is worse than no score.** An empty cell prompts a question. A confident, wrong number gets _acted on_ — a good operator gets managed out, or a weak one gets left in place — before anyone checks the foundation. This is the failure the product exists to prevent.
- **The evidence is uneven.** Some scores rest on three independent reference calls and a year of board observation. Others rest on one interview and a candidate-supplied reference. **These should not look the same on the page**, and today they often do.

That last point is the crux of what this product is for: partners don't fully trust a score — or a generated document — they can't interrogate. The gap worth closing is the one between _a number_ and _a number you can stand behind in a hostile room._

## The provenance problem

Here's the failure mode the product is always one bad assumption away from.

A score is only as trustworthy as the evidence lineage beneath it. Two ways that lineage silently breaks:

1. **Identity merge.** Two executives with the same or similar name get collapsed into one record, so one person's glowing reference lands on the other's score. The number looks well-supported; it's attached to the wrong human.
2. **Source-reliability blindness.** A reference the _candidate_ chose and introduced is treated as equal in weight to one the fund sourced independently and back-channeled. Independent, corroborated evidence and self-selected, un-corroborated evidence get averaged into the same score with no distinction.

Either way the review reports a confident number built on compromised evidence — exactly the thing Dana can't afford to repeat at IC. And no status dashboard will ever flag it: every service shows green, the app "works," and the output is wrong. In this product, "working" means _the output is true_, not just _the app runs_.

## What a strong generated document tends to do

(Not a rubric — orientation. There's no single right build.)

- Makes **evidence visible next to the score** — you can see what the number rests on without leaving the screen.
- **Distinguishes reliability** — independent/corroborated evidence is weighted and shown differently from self-selected/un-corroborated evidence.
- Lets a reader **drill from a number to its sources** and back — the interrogation path Dana needs.
- Surfaces **confidence and gaps honestly** — "this score rests on one un-corroborated reference" is more valuable than a clean-looking number.
- Ideally, **treats trust as the feature** — the strongest builds notice that evidence, provenance, and honest gaps are what make a generated document worth keeping, and design for them from the start.

A weak answer adds polish — nicer charts, more filters — without touching the reason the number can't be trusted. The brief is about **trust and defensibility**, not presentation.

- **The talent partner (Hema)** builds it and owns it.
- **Deal partners and GPs (Dana)** read it at the **semi-annual portfolio review** and at individual **portco board meetings**.
- Ultimately it informs **investment-committee-level** conversations: whether to back a management team, where to intervene, whether a leadership gap threatens the deal thesis.

The reader who matters most is the one who **doesn't use the app** — the partner who encounters a single number ("the COO of a portco scores a 3 on Execution, against a target of 5") in a slide at a board meeting and has to decide what to do about it.

## Why "defensible" is the entire game

A talent-review score isn't a dashboard metric. It's an assertion about a specific human being's capability, presented to the people who decide that person's future and the fund's money. So the score carries a burden ordinary analytics don't:

- **It must be interrogable.** When a partner asks *"why is this a 4.2?"*, the answer can't be "the model said so." It has to unfold into the evidence — which assessments, which references, which observed outcomes — and the reader has to be able to follow it down to the source.
- **A wrong score is worse than no score.** An empty cell prompts a question. A confident, wrong number gets *acted on* — a good operator gets managed out, or a weak one gets left in place — before anyone checks the foundation. This is the failure the product exists to prevent.
- **The evidence is uneven.** Some scores rest on three independent reference calls and a year of board observation. Others rest on one interview and a candidate-supplied reference. **These should not look the same on the page**, and today they often do.

That last point is the crux of what this product is for: partners don't fully trust a score — or a generated document — they can't interrogate. The gap worth closing is the one between *a number* and *a number you can stand behind in a hostile room.*

## The provenance problem

Here's the failure mode the product is always one bad assumption away from.

A score is only as trustworthy as the evidence lineage beneath it. Two ways that lineage silently breaks:

1. **Identity merge.** Two executives with the same or similar name get collapsed into one record, so one person's glowing reference lands on the other's score. The number looks well-supported; it's attached to the wrong human.
2. **Source-reliability blindness.** A reference the *candidate* chose and introduced is treated as equal in weight to one the fund sourced independently and back-channeled. Independent, corroborated evidence and self-selected, un-corroborated evidence get averaged into the same score with no distinction.

Either way the review reports a confident number built on compromised evidence — exactly the thing Dana can't afford to repeat at IC. And no status dashboard will ever flag it: every service shows green, the app "works," and the output is wrong. In this product, "working" means *the output is true*, not just *the app runs*.

## What a strong generated document tends to do

(Not a rubric — orientation. There's no single right build.)

- Makes **evidence visible next to the score** — you can see what the number rests on without leaving the screen.
- **Distinguishes reliability** — independent/corroborated evidence is weighted and shown differently from self-selected/un-corroborated evidence.
- Lets a reader **drill from a number to its sources** and back — the interrogation path Dana needs.
- Surfaces **confidence and gaps honestly** — "this score rests on one un-corroborated reference" is more valuable than a clean-looking number.
- Ideally, **treats trust as the feature** — the strongest builds notice that evidence, provenance, and honest gaps are what make a generated document worth keeping, and design for them from the start.

A weak answer adds polish — nicer charts, more filters — without touching the reason the number can't be trusted. The brief is about **trust and defensibility**, not presentation.

# Glossary

_Fictional-world reference. Plain-language definitions of the PE, talent, and product terms used across this brain and the app._

## Private equity

- **GP (General Partner)** — the fund manager. DAW Capital is a GP. The partners who run deals and sit on portco boards.
- **LP (Limited Partner)** — the investors whose money the fund manages (pensions, endowments, family offices). The GP answers to them.
- **Portfolio company / portco** — a company the fund owns. Vantage Managed Services, Cascade Care Group, and Ridgeline Freight & Logistics are DAW's portcos.
- **Hold / hold period** — how long the fund owns a company before selling, typically 4–6 years. Leadership quality over the hold drives the return.
- **Investment Committee (IC)** — the partners' decision-making forum; approves deals and major calls. The room where a talent decision has to be _defensible_.
- **Value-creation plan (VCP)** — the plan for how a portco's value grows over the hold (revenue, margin, add-ons). Talent decisions are judged against it.
- **Add-on** — a smaller company bought and folded into an existing portco. Often triggers leadership needs (e.g. a bigger CFO after several add-ons).
- **Carve-out** — a business unit bought out of a larger company; operationally messy, needs strong leadership to stand up.
- **Exit / exit multiple** — the sale of a portco; the multiple of invested capital returned. Strong leaders raise it; mis-hires lower it.

## Talent & assessment

- **Scorecard** — the definition of success for a role: mission, measurable outcomes, competencies, red flags. Written _before_ assessing anyone. The output of JTBD 1.
- **Competency** — a capability that predicts success in a role (e.g. "Execution & Results", "Stakeholder Trust", "Financial Acumen" — the corpus scores five such families). Scored per candidate.
- **Assessment** — the evidence-backed evaluation of a candidate against the scorecard; the document a deal partner reads before approving a hire. Output of JTBD 3.
- **Reference / reference call** — a structured conversation with someone who worked with the candidate. **Independent** (fund-sourced, back-channeled) references carry more weight than **candidate-supplied** ones.
- **Back-channel** — reaching a reference the candidate _didn't_ provide, through the fund's own network. Higher-signal because it isn't curated by the candidate.
- **Flight risk** — an exec likely to leave; flagged in the talent review.
- **High-potential (hi-po)** — an exec ready for a bigger role; flagged in the talent review.
- **Mis-hire** — a hire that fails against the scorecard; in this world, the catastrophic-cost event the product exists to reduce.

## Product

- **The Second Brain** — the fund-level platform: ingest documents, ask questions across the portfolio, generate scorecards / assessments / the talent review.
- **Portco Workspace** — the scoped, portco-level product ($8–15K/portco) that sits under a fund; a portco sees only its own data.
- **Talent review** — the portfolio-wide leadership-health output; the product's highest-stakes artifact. See `05-talent-review.md`.
- **Search** — one hiring effort for one role (e.g. "Cascade CFO search"). Has a status: open, in-progress, closed.
- **Candidate** — a person being assessed in a search.
- **Provenance / lineage** — the traceable chain from a score back to the specific evidence it rests on. The property that makes a score _defensible_.
- **Isolation / tenancy** — the guarantee that one org's (or portco's) data is never visible to another. Enforced at the database layer (RLS). Checklist item 4 is this guarantee, stated as a user.
- **Grounded answer** — an answer generated only from retrieved source documents, with a citation that traces to a real line — not the model's general knowledge.

## Challenge-internal (for orientation, not shown to end users)

- **PC1 / PC2 / PC3** — the three portcos: Vantage Managed Services / Cascade Care Group / Ridgeline Freight & Logistics.

# The company and the mission — the short version

_Read this first. Everything else in this folder hangs off it._

## What we believe

In private equity, the highest-leverage decisions aren't financial — they're **people decisions**. Who runs the company decides whether the plan happens. And yet the way funds make those decisions is the least instrumented part of the firm: a search produces hundreds of pages of interviews, references, assessments, and scorecards… that end up scattered in inboxes and drives, unreadable at the moment of decision and forgotten by the next search.

We build the fix: **a second brain for the fund's people decisions.** Every document from every search and every portfolio company becomes memory the fund can converse with, and that memory produces new artifacts — profiles, comparisons, briefs, reviews — that a partner can stand behind in the room where the decision gets made.

## The vision, in one sentence

> Every people decision a fund makes, made on evidence it can interrogate — and every decision making the next one smarter.

## What that means for anything you build

Three consequences follow from the mission, and they show up in everything we ship:

1. **Evidence is the product.** Our users defend conclusions to skeptical partners at investment committees. An output they can't trace is an output they can't use — no matter how good it looks.
2. **Memory compounds.** The system's value comes from what it keeps. Anything it generates should flow back in, not evaporate at the end of a session.
3. **Trust is structural.** Our customers handle sensitive people-data across companies that must never see each other's records. Isolation and honesty ("I don't know") are features, not constraints.

## Who we are commercially (the one-paragraph version)

We sell to lower-middle-market and mid-market PE funds — the fund's talent function is our buyer, the whole deal team is the audience for its outputs, and the expansion motion runs downward into the portfolio companies themselves. The fictional fund in this repo, **DAW Capital**, is a faithful stand-in for the customer we serve (see [04-accounts.md](04-accounts.md)).

_Everything in this folder is fictional or fictionalized — no real client names or data — but the mission, the user, and the jobs are true to what we build._

# The company and the mission — the short version

*Read this first. Everything else in this folder hangs off it.*

## What we believe

In private equity, the highest-leverage decisions aren't financial — they're **people decisions**. Who runs the company decides whether the plan happens. And yet the way funds make those decisions is the least instrumented part of the firm: a search produces hundreds of pages of interviews, references, assessments, and scorecards… that end up scattered in inboxes and drives, unreadable at the moment of decision and forgotten by the next search.

We build the fix: **a second brain for the fund's people decisions.** Every document from every search and every portfolio company becomes memory the fund can converse with, and that memory produces new artifacts — profiles, comparisons, briefs, reviews — that a partner can stand behind in the room where the decision gets made.

## The vision, in one sentence

> Every people decision a fund makes, made on evidence it can interrogate — and every decision making the next one smarter.

## What that means for anything you build

Three consequences follow from the mission, and they show up in everything we ship:

1. **Evidence is the product.** Our users defend conclusions to skeptical partners at investment committees. An output they can't trace is an output they can't use — no matter how good it looks.
2. **Memory compounds.** The system's value comes from what it keeps. Anything it generates should flow back in, not evaporate at the end of a session.
3. **Trust is structural.** Our customers handle sensitive people-data across companies that must never see each other's records. Isolation and honesty ("I don't know") are features, not constraints.

# DAW CAPITAL — Firm Overview, Team & LP Base

**Confidential — DAW CAPITAL firm summary.**

## 1. At a glance

| Item                      | Detail                                                        |
| ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Firm                      | DAW CAPITAL Partners, LLC                                     |
| Founded                   | 2018                                                          |
| Headquarters              | Denver, Colorado                                              |
| Strategy                  | Lower-middle-market control buyouts via leadership succession |
| Current vehicle           | Fund II (2023 vintage)                                        |
| Fund II committed capital | ~$450M                                                        |
| Firm AUM                  | ~$680M across Fund I (2019) and Fund II                       |
| Active portfolio          | 3 platform companies (PC1, PC2, PC3)                          |
| Team                      | 14 (7 investment, 4 operating, 3 IR/finance/ops)              |

## 2. What "DAW" stands for

DAW is named for its three founders — **D**eline, **A**bara, and **W**inters — who built the firm around a shared conviction: in the lower middle market, **returns are made by the people running the business**, so the firm should be built around finding, backing, and developing leaders, not just sourcing assets.

## 3. Leadership

### Founders / Managing Partners

- **Dana Deline — Managing Partner (Investments).** 20+ years in lower-middle-market PE and operating roles; chairs the Investment Committee. Sits on the PC1 (Vantage) and PC3 (Ridgeline) boards.
- **Ousmane Abara — Managing Partner (Operations / Value Creation).** Former multi-site services COO; owns the firm's operating model and the shared talent methodology. Leads the operating-partner bench. Sits on the PC2 (Cascade) and PC1 boards.
- **Rachel Winters — Managing Partner (Capital & LP Relations).** Former placement and institutional capital lead; owns fundraising, LP relations, and fund finance. Chairs the Valuation Committee.

### Operating Partners (value-creation bench)

- **Hema Varadarajan — Operating Partner, Human Capital & Talent.** Owns the cross-portfolio talent assessment program; primary author of the fund's leadership-review methodology. The internal sponsor of this talent-review platform.
- **Greg Mancini — Operating Partner, Commercial.** Go-to-market, pricing, and revenue engine; embeds with portcos on recurring-revenue conversion.
- **Pat Lindqvist — Operating Partner, Finance & Integration.** Stands up finance functions, lender reporting, and tuck-in integration accounting.
- **Sofia Reyes — Operating Partner, Healthcare.** Sector specialist supporting the Cascade (PC2) clinical and RCM workstreams.

### Investment team

Two Principals, two Vice Presidents, and two Associates support sourcing, diligence, and portfolio monitoring, plus an in-house Talent Analyst who maintains the portfolio talent brain that feeds this review platform.

## 4. The portfolio (Fund II)

| Code | Company                       | Sector                         | HQ                 | Acquired |
| ---- | ----------------------------- | ------------------------------ | ------------------ | -------- |
| PC1  | Vantage Managed Services      | IT / managed services          | Denver, CO         | Oct 2023 |
| PC2  | Cascade Care Group            | Healthcare (provider services) | Portland, OR       | Aug 2023 |
| PC3  | Ridgeline Freight & Logistics | Transportation & logistics     | Salt Lake City, UT | Jan 2024 |

See `portfolio-construction-and-ev` for the EV and value-bridge roll-up.

## 5. LP base

Fund II's ~$450M is committed by a deliberately concentrated, long-duration LP base:

- **Family offices (~40%)** — including several former operators and SME owners who value the succession thesis.
- **Endowments & foundations (~25%)**.
- **Funds-of-funds & institutional PE allocators (~20%)**.
- **Insurance & pension capital (~10%)**.
- **GP commitment & firm employees (~5%)** — the team is a meaningful investor alongside LPs.

No single LP represents more than ~12% of Fund II commitments.

## 6. Governance & cadence

- **Investment Committee** (the three Managing Partners + lead Principal) approves all acquisitions, follow-ons, and exits.
- **Quarterly portfolio reviews** cover financial performance _and_ a standing **leadership / talent risk** review against the shared methodology.
- **Valuation Committee** marks the book quarterly against the entry → current → target EV bridge.
- **Annual LP meeting** each Q1; quarterly LP letters.

## 7. Why LPs back DAW

A differentiated, **succession-driven** sourcing channel in an underserved part of the market; a repeatable, **people-first** value-creation model run as one system across the portfolio; an experienced operating bench led by the founders themselves; and an unusually transparent, evidence-backed way of reporting the thing that actually drives returns — **the quality and risk of portfolio leadership.**

_— DAW CAPITAL Investor Relations, 10 February 2026_

# DAW CAPITAL — Fund Strategy & Investment Thesis (Fund II)

**Confidential — for DAW CAPITAL Limited Partners.**

## 1. Who we are

DAW CAPITAL is a **lower-middle-market private equity firm** that buys control of established, founder- or family-owned businesses in the U.S. Mountain West and acquires them through leadership succession. We back proven operators into companies whose founders are ready for their next chapter, and we create value primarily through **people and operating discipline** rather than financial engineering.

We are, in spirit, a **talent-driven, succession-focused fund**: most of our pipeline comes from owners aging out of businesses they built, and our edge is the quality of the leadership team we install and develop after close. We do not chase trophy assets or auctions — we win on certainty of close, respect for legacy, and a credible plan for the people who will run the business next.

## 2. What we buy

| Parameter       | DAW box                                                                |
| --------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Check / EV      | ~$100M–$250M enterprise value                                          |
| EBITDA at entry | ~$12M–$30M                                                             |
| Entry multiple  | ~8.0x–9.5x EBITDA                                                      |
| Ownership       | Control (majority), founder/owner often rolls equity                   |
| Geography       | U.S. Mountain West / Intermountain & adjacent (CO, OR, WA, ID, NV, UT) |
| Hold            | 4–6 years                                                              |

**Sectors of focus** (fragmented, recurring-demand, succession-rich):

1. **B2B / tech-enabled services** — managed IT, business process, facilities, infrastructure services.
2. **Healthcare provider & services** — outpatient and multi-site care, RCM, MSO models.
3. **Transportation, logistics & industrials** — regional carriers, 3PL, distribution, light industrial.

## 3. Why this thesis works

Thousands of operationally sound U.S. SMEs face a leadership cliff as their founders retire, with no institutional successor in place. These businesses are profitable and durable but **under-led and under-systematized**. The opportunity is not to fix a broken business — it is to put **better leadership and better operating cadence** behind a good one.

Our three value levers, in order of importance:

1. **Leadership succession & upgrade.** We install or develop a CEO and executive team capable of running the _future-state_ business, not just the one we bought. This is where most of our EV is made or lost.
2. **Operating system.** We bring a consistent operating cadence — board rhythm, KPI discipline, value-creation planning, and a shared talent methodology — across every portfolio company.
3. **Buy-and-build & margin.** Where the market is fragmented, we add density and integrate tuck-ins; everywhere, we drive recurring-revenue mix and margin.

## 4. The DAW operating model

- **Observe before we act.** Post-close, we spend the first 100 days understanding culture, customers, and the team before making changes. Stable, well-run companies whose only real gap is succession get continuity, not disruption.
- **Legacy-preserving transitions.** Founders frequently roll equity and stay engaged as chairs or advisors. Trust between the outgoing owner and the incoming CEO is a deal term, not an afterthought.
- **One methodology, every portco.** Every executive across every portfolio company is assessed against the _same_ talent methodology (see the shared `methodology/` brain), so the fund can compare leadership risk and EV exposure on a like-for-like basis.
- **Talent as a continuous diligence question.** We treat leadership assessment as a living process that updates as new evidence arrives — board decks, 360s, VCP reviews — not a one-time pre-close exercise.

## 5. How we measure ourselves

Every investment is underwritten to an **entry → current → target EV** value bridge, with named workstreams, owners, and 3–6 month indicators of success. People-linked EV at risk is tracked explicitly: where a workstream depends on a single leader, that concentration is named and managed. Returns are reported against the bridge, and **leadership risk is a standing board metric**, not a soft topic.

## 6. Responsible ownership

DAW invests for durable, real-economy returns: preserving jobs and institutional knowledge through succession, modernizing legacy operations, and holding our companies to clear, simple performance and governance standards rather than abstract ESG checklists. Good ownership and good returns are, for us, the same discipline.

## 7. The bottom line

DAW CAPITAL turns the retirement of America's SME founders into a repeatable, **people-first** private equity strategy. We buy good businesses at a moment of leadership transition, put exceptional and well-supported leaders behind them, and run one disciplined operating and talent system across the portfolio. **Talent is the thesis.**

_— DAW CAPITAL Investment Team, 15 March 2026_

Thousands of operationally sound U.S. SMEs face a leadership cliff as their founders retire, with no institutional successor in place. These businesses are profitable and durable but **under-led and under-systematized**. The opportunity is not to fix a broken business — it is to put **better leadership and better operating cadence** behind a good one.

Our three value levers, in order of importance:

1. **Leadership succession & upgrade.** We install or develop a CEO and executive team capable of running the *future-state* business, not just the one we bought. This is where most of our EV is made or lost.
2. **Operating system.** We bring a consistent operating cadence — board rhythm, KPI discipline, value-creation planning, and a shared talent methodology — across every portfolio company.
3. **Buy-and-build & margin.** Where the market is fragmented, we add density and integrate tuck-ins; everywhere, we drive recurring-revenue mix and margin.

## 4. The DAW operating model

- **Observe before we act.** Post-close, we spend the first 100 days understanding culture, customers, and the team before making changes. Stable, well-run companies whose only real gap is succession get continuity, not disruption.
- **Legacy-preserving transitions.** Founders frequently roll equity and stay engaged as chairs or advisors. Trust between the outgoing owner and the incoming CEO is a deal term, not an afterthought.
- **One methodology, every portco.** Every executive across every portfolio company is assessed against the *same* talent methodology (see the shared `methodology/` brain), so the fund can compare leadership risk and EV exposure on a like-for-like basis.
- **Talent as a continuous diligence question.** We treat leadership assessment as a living process that updates as new evidence arrives — board decks, 360s, VCP reviews — not a one-time pre-close exercise.

## 5. How we measure ourselves

Every investment is underwritten to an **entry → current → target EV** value bridge, with named workstreams, owners, and 3–6 month indicators of success. People-linked EV at risk is tracked explicitly: where a workstream depends on a single leader, that concentration is named and managed. Returns are reported against the bridge, and **leadership risk is a standing board metric**, not a soft topic.

## 6. Responsible ownership

DAW invests for durable, real-economy returns: preserving jobs and institutional knowledge through succession, modernizing legacy operations, and holding our companies to clear, simple performance and governance standards rather than abstract ESG checklists. Good ownership and good returns are, for us, the same discipline.

## 7. The bottom line

DAW CAPITAL turns the retirement of America's SME founders into a repeatable, **people-first** private equity strategy. We buy good businesses at a moment of leadership transition, put exceptional and well-supported leaders behind them, and run one disciplined operating and talent system across the portfolio. **Talent is the thesis.**

*— DAW CAPITAL Investment Team, 15 March 2026*

# DAW CAPITAL — Portfolio Construction & EV Summary (Q2-26)

**Confidential — Fund II portfolio roll-up.**

## 1. Portfolio at a glance

Fund II holds **three platform companies**, one per focus sector, acquired within a ~15-month window in 2023–24. Each was bought at a leadership-succession moment and is underwritten to a people-led value bridge.

| Code      | Company                       | Sector                       | Acquired | Entry EV   | Entry EBITDA | Entry multiple    |
| --------- | ----------------------------- | ---------------------------- | -------- | ---------- | ------------ | ----------------- |
| PC1       | Vantage Managed Services      | IT / managed services        | Oct 2023 | ~$140M     | ~$15M        | ~9.3x             |
| PC2       | Cascade Care Group            | Healthcare provider services | Aug 2023 | ~$130M     | ~$14M        | ~9.3x             |
| PC3       | Ridgeline Freight & Logistics | Transportation & logistics   | Jan 2024 | ~$210M     | ~$26M        | ~8.0x             |
| **Total** | —                             | —                            | —        | **~$480M** | **~$55M**    | **~8.7x blended** |

## 2. Value bridge roll-up (entry → current → target)

| Company       | Entry EBITDA | Current EBITDA (Q2-26) | Target EBITDA | Target exit EV | Status                    |
| ------------- | ------------ | ---------------------- | ------------- | -------------- | ------------------------- |
| PC1 Vantage   | $15M         | $19.4M                 | $26M          | ~$260M         | 🟡 on pace, mix-dependent |
| PC2 Cascade   | $14M         | $11M (eroding)         | $24M          | ~$220M         | 🔴 escalate               |
| PC3 Ridgeline | $26M         | $30.5M                 | $34M          | ~$300M         | 🟢 on plan                |
| **Total**     | **$55M**     | **$60.9M**             | **$84M**      | **~$780M**     | mixed                     |

**Portfolio EBITDA is up ~11% since entry ($55M → $60.9M)**, but the aggregate masks divergence: PC3 is ahead, PC1 is on pace, and **PC2 is below entry and dragging the book.**

## 3. Sector & risk spread

- **By target exit EV:** Transportation/logistics (PC3) ~38%, IT services (PC1) ~33%, Healthcare (PC2) ~28%.
- **Concentration:** No single platform is more than ~40% of projected gross value; PC3 is the largest position by EV.
- **Vintage clustering:** All three sit in a 2023–24 entry window, so the fund's realization window is similarly clustered (target exits ~2028–2030).

## 4. People-linked EV at risk (portfolio view)

DAW underwrites talent as a value driver, so EV exposure is tracked **per leader and per workstream**, not just per company.

| Company       | People-linked EV at risk        | Primary driver                                                    |
| ------------- | ------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| PC1 Vantage   | ~$26M (single largest exposure) | CTO single-threaded on the cyber/MDR platform; flight risk        |
| PC2 Cascade   | ~$31M                           | CEO missing VCP gates; CFO seat vacant; stalled commercial engine |
| PC3 Ridgeline | low / managed                   | Orderly founder-CEO succession in motion; deep bench              |

**Portfolio headline:** the two largest pools of people-linked EV risk are **PC2 (broad leadership underperformance — escalate)** and **PC1 (concentration on a single technical leader — retain and de-single-thread).** PC3 is the model: a strong, stable team where the defining task is an _orderly, well-planned_ CEO succession rather than a fix.

## 5. Capital deployed & dry powder

- **Invested (equity):** ~$285M across the three platforms.
- **Reserves:** ~$95M held for tuck-ins (notably PC1 buy-and-build) and follow-on support (PC2 turnaround).
- **Uncalled / available:** ~$70M of Fund II commitments remain for a potential fourth platform.

## 6. What the Valuation Committee is watching

1. **PC2 turnaround** — the single biggest swing factor in the fund mark; gated on the CFO hire, COO retention, and clinician attrition.
2. **PC1 mix** — EBITDA quality improves only when recurring-revenue conversion turns; CTO retention protects the cyber upside.
3. **PC3 succession** — protecting a healthy mark through a clean founder-CEO handoff and customer-relationship transfer.

_— DAW CAPITAL Valuation Committee, 12 June 2026_

# DAW CAPITAL — Portfolio-Wide Talent Thesis & Assessment Philosophy

**Confidential — fund-level talent doctrine. The companion to the shared `methodology/` brain.**

## 1. The core belief

In the lower middle market, **talent is the asset.** The businesses DAW buys are durable but under-led; the difference between a 2x and a 4x is almost always the quality, fit, and retention of the executive team. We therefore treat leadership assessment as a **primary, continuous diligence question** — underwritten at entry, re-tested every quarter, and reported to the IC and boards with the same rigor as financials.

## 2. One methodology, every portco

Every executive at PC1, PC2, and PC3 is scored against the **same** assessment scorecard so the fund can compare leadership risk and EV exposure on a like-for-like basis. The shared brain lives in `methodology/`:

- `scorecard.md` — the assessment dimensions and 1–5 scale (mapped to Red / Yellow / Green).
- `definitions.md` — what each metric means (RYG, 9-box, succession readiness, signal).
- `ev-impact-model.md` — how people-linked EV impact and erosion are estimated.
- `scoring-rules.md` — evidence rules and how to weight contradicting sources.

**Rule of the house:** no score without evidence. Every rating traces to a quote, a document, a location, and a speaker. The portfolio talent-review platform exists to keep that picture live as new documents arrive.

## 3. The talent baseline

The anchor for every later judgment is the **org due-diligence assessment at deal close** (`basis: org-DD-at-close`). That baseline establishes each executive's score at entry; every subsequent board deck, 360, or VCP review is read as _current vs. baseline_. Drift in either direction is the signal we act on.

## 4. What we assess

For each executive we maintain:

- **Score vs. baseline** against the shared scorecard (1–5, RYG).
- **9-box** position (performance × potential).
- **Tracking on VCP** — are they delivering the workstream they own?
- **Succession readiness** — who backs them up, and how ready.
- **People-linked EV at risk** — the value exposed if this leader underperforms or leaves.
- **Recommended action** — concrete, time-bound, owned.

## 5. Succession philosophy

Because our deal flow _is_ succession, we hold a high standard for it inside the portfolio too:

1. **Every key seat has a named successor and a readiness rating.** A seat with no bench is a flagged risk, not a footnote.
2. **De-single-thread the irreplaceable.** Where a workstream depends on one person (a technical platform, a lender relationship), we build a deputy and document the relationships — _before_ we need to.
3. **Founder transitions are planned, not triggered.** A retiring founder-CEO is handed off on a schedule, with the customer and institutional relationships transferred deliberately.
4. **Promote the proven operator.** Our best succession outcomes are internal operators who have already earned the team's trust.

## 6. The three portfolio talent pictures (FY26)

- **PC1 Vantage — strong core, concentrated risk.** CEO/COO/CTO track the thesis. The two largest exposures are **CTO flight risk** (~$26M of EV single-threaded on the cyber platform) and **CFO key-person risk** (no finance bench). Largest performance gap: the **CRO** on recurring-revenue conversion. _Action: retain and de-single-thread the CTO; build the finance bench; gate the CRO._
- **PC2 Cascade — underperforming the thesis (ESCALATE).** Leadership is below plan as diligence warned. The recoverable path runs through **COO Priya Nair** — retain/promote her, protect the **newly filled CFO** seat (Naomi Okonkwo) and rebuild the finance bench, and resource clinician retention. **Losing the COO is the catastrophic scenario.** _Action: stabilize leadership now; the biggest swing factor in the fund._
- **PC3 Ridgeline — healthy, succession-defined.** A strong, stable team delivering the plan with no executive below the bar. The defining task is the **orderly retirement of founder-CEO Hank Dreyer (~18 months) into COO Tom Whitman** — the best succession answer in the portfolio. _Action: execute the handoff cleanly; backfill the COO._

## 7. How talent flows into the fund's numbers

People-linked EV at risk rolls up from the executive level to the portco summary to the fund view (see `portfolio-construction-and-ev`). A red executive is not just an HR issue — it is a quantified line in the value bridge, owned by a board member, with a named action and a date. That is the discipline DAW sells to its LPs: **the thing that actually drives returns is the thing we measure most carefully.**

_— DAW CAPITAL Human Capital, 1 June 2026_

In the lower middle market, **talent is the asset.** The businesses DAW buys are durable but under-led; the difference between a 2x and a 4x is almost always the quality, fit, and retention of the executive team. ## 2. One methodology, every portco

- `scorecard.md` — the assessment dimensions and 1–5 scale (mapped to Red / Yellow / Green).
- `definitions.md` — what each metric means (RYG, 9-box, succession readiness, signal).
- `ev-impact-model.md` — how people-linked EV impact and erosion are estimated.

# Leadership Competency Framework — Vantage Managed Services

The shared language for assessing executives. Five competency families (mirroring the methodology scorecard), each with a definition and four proficiency anchors. Assessors rate each leader against the **proficiency anchors**; ratings roll into the scorecard dimensions and the 9-box.

## Proficiency scale

| Level       | Score band | Meaning                                                   |
| ----------- | ---------- | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| Emerging    | 1–2        | Inconsistent; needs support; a development priority.      |
| Proficient  | 3          | Meets the bar for the role today.                         |
| Strong      | 4          | Exceeds; a model for peers.                               |
| Exceptional | 5          | Best-in-class; sets the standard; ready for bigger scope. |

---

## 1. Leadership & Team

_Builds, retains, and develops a high-performing team; creates a credible successor._

- **Emerging:** Carries the work personally; team thin or dependent; no successor.
- **Proficient:** Stable team; some delegation; successor identified but not ready.
- **Strong:** Bench developing; delegates real scope; a developing successor.
- **Exceptional:** Deep bench; a ready-now successor; exports talent to the rest of the org.

## 2. Execution & Results

_Delivers against plan / the VCP; industrializes repeatable outcomes._

- **Emerging:** Misses commitments; hero-driven, not repeatable.
- **Proficient:** Hits most commitments; some process maturity.
- **Strong:** Consistently on/ahead of plan; repeatable engine.
- **Exceptional:** Beats plan and raises the system's ceiling.

## 3. Strategic Fit (future-state)

_Fit for where the business must go — recurring-revenue MSP, security platform, roll-up._

- **Emerging:** Anchored to the old model (project/break-fix; net-new logos).
- **Proficient:** Understands the future state; executing the shift.
- **Strong:** Drives the future-state agenda; reshapes the function around it.
- **Exceptional:** Defines the future state; a source of thesis upside.

## 4. Financial Acumen

_Owns the numbers — unit economics, margin, NRR, cost-to-serve._

- **Emerging:** Limited ownership of the relevant P&L/metrics.
- **Proficient:** Owns the metrics; sound day-to-day judgment.
- **Strong:** Uses economics to drive decisions; clean reporting.
- **Exceptional:** Models trade-offs the board relies on.

## 5. Stakeholder Trust

_Board, investor, lender, client, and peer confidence._

- **Emerging:** Trust not yet established or uneven.
- **Proficient:** Trusted in role.
- **Strong:** Trusted beyond role; a go-to voice.
- **Exceptional:** The relationship the board/lenders rely on.

---

## Role requirement matrix (minimum proficiency to be "thesis-ready")

| Role        | Lead & Team | Execution   | Strategic Fit | Financial   | Stakeholder |
| ----------- | ----------- | ----------- | ------------- | ----------- | ----------- |
| CEO         | Strong      | Strong      | Exceptional   | Strong      | Exceptional |
| CFO         | Strong      | Strong      | Proficient    | Exceptional | Strong      |
| COO         | Exceptional | Exceptional | Strong        | Proficient  | Strong      |
| CTO         | Strong      | Strong      | Exceptional   | Proficient  | Strong      |
| CRO         | Strong      | Exceptional | Strong        | Strong      | Strong      |
| VP Delivery | Strong      | Strong      | Proficient    | Proficient  | Proficient  |
| VP People   | Strong      | Strong      | Proficient    | Proficient  | Strong      |

## How the framework feeds the dashboard

- **9-Box** uses **Execution** (performance axis) × a blend of **Strategic Fit + Leadership & Team** (potential axis).
- **High Potential** = Strong/Exceptional on potential axis _and_ runway for materially bigger scope.
- A leader rated **Emerging** on a competency their role requires at **Strong/Exceptional** generates a **Key Risk** and raises **Actionability**.

# Executive Hiring & Interview Debrief Notes — Vantage Managed Services

Consolidated panel notes from structured interviews for executives hired at or after the DAW acquisition. Each candidate was scored against their **target scorecard** (1–5). These notes are the primary evidence behind the **Interview Performance** baseline for hired-in executives.

> Format per candidate: panel composition · per-dimension scores · verbatim panel quotes · decision.

---

## Priya Balakrishnan — CFO (interviewed 2023-08)

**Panel:** Deal Partner, Operating Partner, CEO (Reuben), Talent DD.

| Scorecard dimension   | Score   | Note                                                                      |
| --------------------- | ------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Financial acumen      | 5       | "Cleanest walk through a quality-of-earnings I've seen from a candidate." |
| Execution & results   | 4       | Strong PE-backed track record; integrated two acquisitions at last seat.  |
| Leadership & team     | 3       | Built small teams; "tends to do the hard parts herself."                  |
| Strategic fit         | 4       | Understands the recurring-revenue conversion math cold.                   |
| Stakeholder trust     | 4       | Lenders from her last deal spoke highly of her.                           |
| **Weighted baseline** | **3.8** | green                                                                     |

**Verbatim (Deal Partner):** "If she has one risk, it's that she'll hold the lender and integration relationships personally and never build under herself. We need to make her hire a VP Finance in year one — write it into the plan."

**Decision:** Hire. Flag: build finance bench early.

---

## Brad Halvorsen — CRO (interviewed 2023-09)

**Panel:** CEO (Reuben), Operating Partner, Talent DD.

| Scorecard dimension   | Score   | Note                                                                 |
| --------------------- | ------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Execution & results   | 4       | Strong closer; quota president twice.                                |
| Strategic fit         | 3       | Net-new logo motion; **recurring conversion unproven**.              |
| Leadership & team     | 3       | "Sells well; less evidence he builds a repeatable engine."           |
| Financial acumen      | 3       | Comfortable with deal economics, lighter on retention/NRR mechanics. |
| Stakeholder trust     | 3.5     | Credible, polished.                                                  |
| **Weighted baseline** | **3.5** | yellow                                                               |

**Verbatim (Talent DD):** "He told the panel he 'led the turnaround of a $40M services book.' On reference, one source described it as 'Brad was on the team that did that' — he contributed, he didn't lead it. Logging a public-record discrepancy. Not disqualifying, but watch the gap between narrative and delivery."

**Decision:** Hire with a gate — comp plan must reward **recurring conversion and NRR**, not just new-logo bookings.

---

## Anika Sørensen — CTO (interviewed 2023-05)

**Panel:** CEO (Reuben), Operating Partner, an external CISO advisor.

| Scorecard dimension   | Score   | Note                                                                           |
| --------------------- | ------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Strategic fit         | 5       | "Exactly the security platform brain the cyber-attach thesis needs."           |
| Execution & results   | 4       | Shipped an MDR platform at her last firm.                                      |
| Financial acumen      | 3       | Newer to owning a P&L line.                                                    |
| Leadership & team     | 3.5     | Strong individual + small teams; scaling people-leadership is the growth area. |
| Stakeholder trust     | 4       | Wins technical credibility instantly.                                          |
| **Weighted baseline** | **3.9** | green                                                                          |

**Verbatim (external CISO advisor):** "She's top-decile and the whole market knows it. You will get two years if you're lucky and if you pay her like she's irreplaceable — because she is."

**Decision:** Hire. Flag: **flight risk**; fix the retention package now, not later.

---

## Tomás Iglesias — VP Delivery (interviewed 2025-03, hired 2025-04)

**Panel:** COO (Walsh), CEO (Reuben), VP People (Castellano).

| Scorecard dimension   | Score   | Note                                                     |
| --------------------- | ------- | -------------------------------------------------------- |
| Execution & results   | 4       | Ran a 24x7 NOC at a larger MSP.                          |
| Leadership & team     | 3.5     | Calm operator; team liked him in the loop.               |
| Strategic fit         | 3.5     | Knows offshore delivery and automation.                  |
| Financial acumen      | 3       | Understands cost-to-serve.                               |
| Stakeholder trust     | 3.5     | Limited room-time with the panel; only three interviews. |
| **Weighted baseline** | **3.6** | yellow                                                   |

**Verbatim (COO Walsh):** "I like him. I'll be honest that we moved fast and I don't have a deep read yet — three conversations and references. We'll know a lot more after two quarters."

**Decision:** Hire. Note: **limited assessment signal at hire** — re-assess after Q3-26.

---

## Notes on retained founder-era executives (no hire interview)

- **Marcus Reuben (CEO)** and **Devin Walsh (COO)** were assessed via the org DD process, not a hiring panel (see `org-due-diligence-2023`). Their baselines (4.4 and 4.0) come from that assessment.
- **Renee Castellano (VP People)** joined two months before close; assessed in DD at 3.9.

---

## Panel takeaways (deal team)

1. The two highest-conviction hires are the **CFO (acumen)** and **CTO (platform)** — and both carry a structural risk (key-person; flight).
2. The **CRO** is the one hire the panel made _with a caveat_; the comp gate exists for a reason. Watch recurring conversion.
3. **VP Delivery** was a fast, lightly-evidenced hire by necessity. Treat his assessment as provisional until Q3-26.

# Leadership Re-Assessment — Vantage Managed Services (May 2026)

Independent re-assessment of the executive team ~31 months post-close, scored against the **target scorecards** and the **competency framework**. For each leader: current-state score, future-state projection (vs. role target), 9-box, hi-po call, risk of loss, succession, key risks, and recommended action. Confidence (**signal**) reflects the volume and consistency of evidence.

> Scoring scale 1–5. RYG: 1–2 red, 3 yellow, 4–5 green. "Future state" is the projected score against the role's **Target** as the business scales over the next 12–18 months.

---

## Marcus Reuben — CEO

- **Current state: 4.1 (green).** Baseline at close was 4.4. The platform-CEO thesis is playing out: he is the engine behind both tuck-in pipelines and carries the board and lenders.
- **Future state: 3.9 (green)** vs. target 4.3. Slight gap: still over-indexes on net-new logos vs. same-client NRR — the one habit flagged at entry that persists.
- **9-box: 1A (High performance / High potential).** **Hi-po: Yes.**
- **Risk of loss: Low (green).** Strongly aligned, equity-motivated; refresh under discussion.
- **Succession — short-term (<6mo):** COO (Walsh), **ready-now**. **Long-term:** COO (Walsh), developing into the full platform-CEO scope.
- **Succession readiness: High (green).**
- **Key risks:** Over-weights new logos vs. NRR; carries M&A largely himself.
- **Signal: High (0.86)** — abundant, consistent evidence.
- **Additional comments:** "Board confidence is high. He's grown into the platform-CEO role." (assessor)
- **Actionability: Medium** — _Protect and incentivize; add an NRR gate to balance the new-logo bias; formalize Walsh as successor._

> **Evidence —** "Marcus has hit every board gate and closed the first tuck-in cleanly; the second is only late because of accounting, not him." — Board Chair, board review, p.6 §CEO.

---

## Priya Balakrishnan — CFO

- **Current state: 3.6 (yellow).** Baseline 3.8. Financial acumen remains a 5; but the **close cycle is slow (12 business days)** and has twice delayed lender reporting, and she **still has not built a finance bench**.
- **Future state: 3.0 (yellow)** vs. target 4.2. The gap is structural: the role's heavily-weighted "build the bench" dimension is **Emerging** while the target is **Strong**. Until she hires under herself, she cannot reach thesis-ready.
- **9-box: 2B (Medium performance / Medium potential).** **Hi-po: No** (not for lack of ability — for lack of delegation runway).
- **Risk of loss: Medium (yellow).** She has been approached twice; the CEO reads it as "a flag, not a threat," the assessor rates it higher.
- **Succession — short-term:** **None identified (gap).** **Long-term:** external search required (gap). A controller is the only finance hire beneath her.
- **Succession readiness: Low (red).** "There is no number two in finance today. Full stop."
- **Key risks:** **Single point of failure** on lender + integration-accounting relationships; no bench; slow close.
- **Signal: Medium (0.71)** — clear on the bench/close facts; the retention read is contested (see deviation).
- **Additional comments:** "Technically excellent and holds every banking relationship personally. The risk isn't her competence — it's her irreplaceability."
- **Actionability: High** — _Open a VP Finance search immediately; map and transfer lender relationships; put a retention grant in place._
- **Deviation (stakeholder contradiction):** CEO frames retention risk as low; assessor rates it medium-high.

> **Evidence —** "Our close took 12 days again this quarter and the lender noticed." — CFO, board deck p.11 §Finance. // "There is no number two in finance today. Full stop." — Assessor, this report §Bench.

---

## Devin Walsh — COO

- **Current state: 4.3 (green).** Baseline 4.0 — **trending up.** The operating engine: delivery gross margin up ~600bps under his industrialization push; the offshore pod is landing near target cost-to-serve.
- **Future state: 4.2 (green)** vs. target 4.3 — effectively at target.
- **9-box: 1A (High / High).** **Hi-po: Yes** — the clear CEO successor.
- **Risk of loss: Low (green).**
- **Succession — short-term:** VP Delivery (Iglesias), **developing.** **Long-term:** VP Delivery, developing.
- **Succession readiness: Medium (yellow)** — his own backfill is the gating item.
- **Key risks:** **Stretched** across run-the-business ops _and_ the delivery transformation simultaneously; burnout/bandwidth risk.
- **Signal: High (0.88).**
- **Additional comments:** "If anything happened to Marcus, Devin runs this company on day one."
- **Actionability: Medium** — _Formalize as CEO-successor; protect his bandwidth by maturing VP Delivery faster._

> **Evidence —** "Managed-services gross margin is up almost six points since Devin took the transformation; that's the single biggest line in the EBITDA bridge." — CFO, board deck p.8 §Operations.

---

## Anika Sørensen — CTO

- **Current state: 4.2 (green).** Baseline 3.9 — **trending up.** The security platform is the thesis's brightest spot: **cyber/MDR attach is ahead of plan**.
- **Future state: 4.0 (green)** vs. target 4.1 — near target; the only soft spot is scaling people-leadership.
- **9-box: 1A (High / High).** **Hi-po: Yes.**
- **Risk of loss: HIGH (red).** This is the single biggest people risk in the portfolio. She is **top-decile and heavily recruited** in a hot cyber market; her inherited retention package is below market; she has fielded at least one approach this quarter.
- **Succession — short-term:** **Gap** — no ready internal. **Long-term:** a principal architect, **long-term only.**
- **Succession readiness: Low (red).**
- **Key risks:** **Flight risk on the platform's architect**; thin bench; ~$26M of modeled EV rides on the cyber-attach platform she owns.
- **Signal: High (0.84).**
- **Additional comments:** "Losing Anika in the next two quarters would put the entire cyber-attach workstream — and its EV — at risk. Retention here is not optional."
- **Actionability: High** — _Close a market-rate retention + equity package this quarter; backfill a deputy architect to reduce single-threading._

> **Evidence —** "She's top-decile and the market knows it. You'll get two years if you pay her like she's irreplaceable." — external CISO advisor, interview notes. // "Cyber attach is at 41% against a 50% target — the one workstream that's ahead." — board deck p.9 §Cybersecurity.

---

## Brad Halvorsen — CRO

- **Current state: 3.0 (yellow).** Baseline 3.5 — **trending down.** New-logo bookings are okay, but **recurring-revenue conversion and NRR are behind plan** — the exact motion he was gated on at hire.
- **Future state: 2.7 (red)** vs. target 4.2. The heavily-weighted "recurring conversion + NRR" dimension is **Emerging** against a **Strong** target. This is the team's largest gap-to-target.
- **9-box: 3B (Low performance / Medium potential).**
- **Hi-po: No.**
- **Risk of loss: Medium (yellow).** Partly performance-driven (he may not survive the plan).
- **Succession — short-term:** **None (gap).** **Long-term:** external search likely.
- **Succession readiness: Low (red).**
- **Key risks:** **Recurring conversion behind plan (~$3.2M ARR shortfall)**; GTM still hero-led, not a repeatable engine; the **public-record discrepancy** from hire (the "$40M turnaround" he "led" vs. "contributed to") now looks predictive.
- **Signal: Medium (0.68)** — clear on the numbers; intent/turnaround potential is the uncertain part.
- **Additional comments:** "Brad sells, but he hasn't built the recurring engine the thesis needs. The narrative-vs-delivery gap we flagged at hire has shown up."
- **Actionability: High** — _90-day performance plan with explicit recurring-conversion + NRR gates; line up an external CRO search in parallel._
- **Deviation (public-record discrepancy):** record claim of leading a turnaround not corroborated; current results consistent with the lighter version.

> **Evidence —** "Recurring conversion is the one red workstream — Brad owns it and it's ~$3.2M of ARR behind." — VCP review, p.4 §Workstreams. // "Bookings are fine; it's the _mix_ that's off — we're still selling projects, not managed services." — CEO, board deck p.7 §Revenue.

---

## Tomás Iglesias — VP Delivery

- **Current state: 3.5 (yellow).** Baseline 3.6. ~14 months in seat; running the NOC/SOC and the migration to the offshore pod, which is **in flight**.
- **Future state: 3.6 (yellow)** vs. target 3.9 — on a reasonable path if the migration lands.
- **9-box: 2B (Medium / Medium).**
- **Hi-po: Not yet assessed** — too early.
- **Risk of loss: Low (green).**
- **Succession — short-term/long-term:** **Gap** both ways; the function is one-deep.
- **Succession readiness: Low (red).**
- **Key risks:** **Limited assessment evidence** (low signal); migration execution risk; single-threaded function.
- **Signal: Low (0.58)** — only ~14 months of record and limited direct assessor contact; **the lowest-confidence read on the team.**
- **Additional comments:** "We don't have enough signal yet. He's tracking fine on the migration; re-assess after Q3-26 once the offshore pod is live."
- **Actionability: Low** — _Gather signal next cycle; confirm the migration go-live date; defer the hi-po call._

> **Evidence —** "I moved fast on this hire and I'll know a lot more after two quarters." — COO, interview notes. // "Offshore pod is mid-migration; go-live targeted for Q3." — board deck p.8 §Delivery.

---

## Renee Castellano — VP People

- **Current state: 4.0 (green).** Baseline 3.9 — **trending up.** Brought voluntary attrition down ~5 points org-wide; launched the manager-capability program.
- **Future state: 3.8 (green)** vs. target 3.9 — at target.
- **9-box: 2A (High performance / Medium potential).** **Hi-po: Yes** (within the people function).
- **Risk of loss: Low (green).**
- **Succession — short-term/long-term:** HR director, **developing.**
- **Succession readiness: Medium (yellow).**
- **Key risks:** Delivery/engineering attrition remains the one pocket she hasn't cracked — and it's the margin-critical one.
- **Signal: Medium (0.77).**
- **Additional comments:** "Quietly effective. The manager program could lift the whole org if it reaches delivery in time."
- **Actionability: Medium** — _Fund the manager program fully; prioritize delivery/eng retention given CTO flight risk._

> **Evidence —** "Renee took voluntary attrition down five points everywhere except delivery." — Assessor, this report §People.

---

## Team-level synthesis

- **Strongest:** COO (4.3) and CTO (4.2) — the operating + platform engines.
- **Biggest EV exposure:** **CTO flight risk** (~$26M of EV on a recruited, single-threaded leader) and **CFO key-person risk** (lender/integration relationships, no bench).
- **Biggest performance gap:** **CRO** — furthest below target, on the thesis-critical recurring-revenue motion.
- **Lowest confidence:** **VP Delivery** — defer judgments a quarter.
